items.title: Victor Wembanyama has turned his NBA finals humiliation into a revenge tour for the ages
items.summary:
After a humiliating NBA finals defeat, the 22-year-old has returned with a vengeance – and the Spurs look like contenders again

It wouldn’t be exactly right to say Victor Wembanyama didn’t miss a beat after a disastrous NBA finals in June that left him and his San Antonio Spurs defeated, memed and embarrassed. In the Spurs’ first game this season, against an Oklahoma City Thunder team since decimated by injuries, Wemby went an appalling 1-for-13 from the field. Ten of his 12 points came via free throws. After getting blocked by Aday Mara, he leaned over his knees and muttered furiously to himself as if trying to exorcise an intrusive thought. It brought to mind an image from the NBA finals a few months earlier: Wemby on the floor after being fouled by the Knicks’ Mitchell Robinson, crowing, “I’m in your head!” The Spurs went on to blow a 29-point lead, lose the game and the finals. Now Wemby seemed too preoccupied with the issues within his own dome to worry about wreaking havoc in anybody else’s.

Game two saw Wembanyama elect to lay the ball up instead of dunking it in the dying seconds of a close tilt with the Houston Rockets, which the springy Amen Thompson blocked spectacularly. Not a great start, and in a league whose narratives calcify long before sample sizes reach an adequate scale, it allowed for whispers that the Spurs were in trouble. But you could say Wembanyama has not missed…
items.t: Victor Wembanyama has turned his NBA finals humiliation into a revenge tour for the ages

items.title: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent
items.summary:
The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric

Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black.

“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.summary:
Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys

After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. Simon Burnton

items.title: Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn
items.summary:
Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle

Who said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay. SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum”, announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled.

Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr, had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account. But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction.
items.t: Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn

items.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
items.summary:
Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

items.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
items.summary:
Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled

Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast.

Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-life business proposition; a legitimate going concern with profits and a bottom line and a plan for the future.
